parts.title: Campus Conversation: Visiting a Professor's Office Hours
script: Narrator
Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor.
Woman
Hi, Professor Brown. Do you have a minute?
Man
Of course. Please come in. It is my office hour.
Woman
Thank you. I have a question about the history paper. I do not understand the topic.
Man
Okay. The paper is about a famous city in the past. You can choose Rome, Athens, or Cairo.
Woman
I think I like Rome. How long should the paper be?
Man
It should be five pages. It is due next Friday.
Woman
Next Friday? I thought it was due this Friday. That is good news.
Man
Yes, you have one more week. But please start early. You should read two books about the city.
Woman
Can I find the books in the library?
Man
Yes. You can also borrow my book about Rome. I will give it to you now.
Woman
Thank you so much. I will bring it back next week.
Man
Good. If you have more questions, send me an email.

questions.q: Why does the student visit the professor?
questions.exp: She has a question about the history paper.

questions.q: Which city does the student want to write about?

questions.exp: The professor says it is due next Friday.

questions.q: Listen again: "But please start early." Why does the professor say this?
o: He wants her to begin the paper soon
He wants to close the office
He wants her to come early to class
He wants her to buy a book
questions.exp: He wants her to start working early.

questions.q: How does the student probably feel at the end?
questions.exp: She says thank you and is glad about the extra week.

parts.title: Academic Lecture: How Do Penguins Stay Warm?
script: Narrator
Listen to part of a lecture in a biology class.
Professor
Today we will talk about penguins. Penguins live in very cold places, like Antarctica. The air there can be very cold, and the wind is strong. So how do penguins stay warm?
Professor
First, penguins have a thick layer of fat under their skin. This fat works like a warm coat. It keeps the heat inside the body.
Professor
Second, penguins have very small, tight feathers. The feathers cover the whole body. They keep the cold water and wind away from the skin.
Professor

Third, penguins stand close together in a big group. This is called a huddle. The penguins in the middle are warm. After some time, the penguins on the outside move to the middle. In this way, every penguin gets a turn to be warm.
Professor
Some people think penguins are only found on ice. But this is not true. Some penguins live in warmer places, such as South Africa. Still, most of them live in cold areas.
Professor
So, remember: fat, feathers, and huddling. These are three ways penguins stay warm. Next time, we will talk about how penguins find food.

questions.q: What is the lecture mainly about?
questions.exp: The professor explains how penguins stay warm.

questions.q: What does the layer of fat under the skin do?
o: It keeps heat inside the body
questions.exp: Fat works like a warm coat.

questions.q: What do the small, tight feathers do?
o: They keep cold water and wind away
questions.exp: They keep water and wind away from the skin.

o: A group of penguins standing close together
questions.exp: A huddle is a big group standing close together.

questions.q: Listen again: "In this way, every penguin gets a turn to be warm." Why does the professor say this?
o: To explain why penguins change places
To say some penguins are lazy
questions.exp: Outside penguins move to the middle, so everyone gets warm.

questions.q: What will the professor probably talk about next time?
questions.exp: He says the next topic is how penguins find food.
